name: Evaluating a nested cell formula
brief:
A risk sheet stores cell formulas built from whole numbers and three functions: `SUM`, `MAX` and `MIN`. Each function takes one or more arguments, separated by commas, and an argument is a number or another call. A number may start with `-`. Spaces may appear between any two parts. The whole formula is a number or one call.

Write `formula_value(formula)`, which returns its value as an `int`.

Example. `"SUM(3, MAX(2, 7), -4)"` is $3 + 7 - 4$, so the answer is 6.
constraints: $1 \le$ `len(formula)` $\le 600{,}000$ characters, always well formed; calls may nest 100,000 deep.
$O(n)$ time is the target. A recursive parser runs out of call depth on deep nesting, and `eval` refuses it.
All the tests in a run share one 5-second limit in the browser.
hint: Push a frame (the function name and an empty argument list) at each opening bracket. At a closing bracket, pop the frame, apply its function and add the result to the frame below.

examples.note: A function may take one argument; the minus belongs to the number.

how: Submit runs 13 hidden tests. Each answer must equal the expected value.
notes: Each open call is a frame on an explicit stack, so the nesting depth costs memory, not call depth.
A minus sign starts a number; it is never an operator here, so it must stay with the digits.
Each character is read once and each value is added to one frame, so the work is $O(n)$.

planted.slip: It parses by recursion, which runs out of call depth when calls nest thousands deep.
It hands the text to `eval`, which cannot take `MAX` of one number and refuses deep nesting.
It skips the minus sign as if it were a separator, so every number reads as positive.
